title: Off the Record
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 8 of 40
content:
Danse asked to speak to me off the record.

This was funny because I had never once seen him write anything on a record while talking to me.

I said so.

He gave me the look.

By then I had categorized several Danse looks.

There was the command look, which meant someone was about to receive an instruction whether they wanted one or not. The tactical look meant he had noticed danger before everyone else. The disappointed look meant Rhys had done something reckless. The particularly rare soft look appeared whenever Haylen fixed something nobody thought could be fixed.

The one he gave me now meant I was making a serious conversation difficult on purpose.

I stopped smiling.

“Sorry.”

He glanced toward the main room.

Haylen and Rhys were arguing about inventory. Neither was paying attention to us.

Danse led me into the back office and shut the door.

“This isn’t disciplinary,” he said.

“I wasn’t worried until you clarified.”

He sighed.

“I wanted to apologize.”

That got my attention.

“For?”

“When we met, I expected you to operate by Brotherhood standards without giving you any reason to understand them.”

I stared.

“You’ve been thinking about this?”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“That’s not relevant.”

“Meaning long enough to be embarrassing.”

His eyes narrowed.

“I’m trying to say something.”

I lifted both hands.

“All right. Go ahead.”

He stood in front of the desk like it was a briefing.

Then nothing came out.

Danse looked toward the window. Back at me. Toward the floor.

I realized with a jolt that he was nervous.

Paladin Danse, who had stood under a rocket engine and ordered me to fire it, was frightened of a personal conversation.

The discovery did not make me want to laugh.

It made me want to be careful.

“You don’t owe me a speech,” I said.

“I know.”

“You can just talk.”

“I am talking.”

“Technically.”

His mouth twitched.

Then the tension in his shoulders eased a fraction.

“I grew up in the Capital Wasteland,” he said. “Orphaned. Mostly scavenged ruins, sold what I could find.”

I stayed quiet.

“When I was older, I saved enough caps to set up a junk stand in Rivet City. That’s where I met Cutler.”

The name was new.

His voice changed around it.

“We watched each other’s backs. Kept each other out of trouble. When the Brotherhood started recruiting, we joined together.”

“Best friend?”

Danse looked uncomfortable with the phrase.

“Yes.”

I sat on the edge of the desk.

“What happened?”

He breathed in slowly.

“About a year after we were posted to the Prydwen, Cutler’s team disappeared.”

“Prydwen?”

“Our airship.”

“You have an airship.”

“That’s what you took from the sentence?”

“I’ll be impressed later.”

He shook his head, but the moment of humor helped.

“I convinced my commanding officer to authorize a search. Took three weeks. We finally tracked them to a super mutant nest.”

His hands closed into fists at his sides.

“The others were dead. Cutler wasn’t.”

I knew before he said it.

“The mutants had exposed him to FEV. He was changing.”

The room felt smaller.

“What did you do?”

Danse looked directly at me.

“I killed him.”

There was no attempt to soften it.

No mercy-kill language. No duty.

Just the fact.

I swallowed.

“I’m sorry.”

“Everyone says that.”

“What should they say?”

“I don’t know.”

His anger flickered, then collapsed into something older.

“I told myself there wasn’t a choice. Brotherhood protocol was clear. FEV transformation is irreversible. Super mutants are dangerous.”

“You still think that.”

“Yes.”

“But?”

He looked away.

“I don’t know if he understood what was happening. I don’t know how much of him was still there when I…”

His voice stopped.

This was not doctrine anymore.

It was grief.

I stood but did not move closer.

“Did he attack you?”

“No.”

“Did he ask you to do it?”

“No.”

Danse’s face hardened as if he expected judgment.

I did not give him absolution either.

“That sounds like something you may never know was right.”

His eyes met mine.

The tension in the room changed.

Most people, I realized, probably told him he had done what was necessary.

Brotherhood people certainly did.

“You think I was wrong.”

“I think you loved your friend and had seconds to make a decision no one should have to make.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No.”

He stared at me.

Then, slowly, some of the anger went out of him.

“Fair.”

I waited.

“After Cutler,” he said, “I stopped getting close to people.”

I thought of the dead lockers.

“Because soldiers die.”

“Everyone dies.”

“That’s cheerful.”

“It’s true.”

“And distance fixes that?”

“No.”

The answer came so quietly I almost missed it.

He leaned against the desk beside me.

“It just makes the loss less…”

“Personal?”

“Yes.”

I looked at his profile.

The strong nose. Dark stubble. A small line between his brows that seemed permanently carved there by responsibility.

“And how’s that working?”

He glanced toward the door where Haylen’s voice rose in irritation at Rhys.

“Poorly.”

I smiled.

Danse did too.

This one lasted.

Then he looked at me and the smile faded into something more uncertain.

“You’re becoming difficult to categorize.”

“That sounds serious.”

“It is.”

“What are the categories?”

“Civilian. Contractor. Potential recruit.”

“And?”

He hesitated.

“Friend.”

The word landed with more force than it deserved.

I knew then what it cost him.

Not because he had said it dramatically.

Because he had not.

Danse treated friendship like ammunition: valuable, limited, not spent carelessly.

I bumped my shoulder lightly against his.

“Careful, Paladin.”

He looked down at the point of contact.

“About what?”

“You’re getting sentimental.”

“I am not.”

“Off the record?”

He groaned.

It was the closest thing to laughter I had heard from him.

When we left the office, Haylen looked between us with open curiosity.

Rhys scowled as a matter of principle.

Danse returned immediately to checking supply manifests as if he had not just handed me one of the most painful pieces of himself.

I picked up Righteous Authority and went to clean it.

The rifle had been his.

The story had been his.

The trust, somehow, was mine now too.

I handled both carefully.

He tested the trust two days later without meaning to.

A Brotherhood distress code came through the repaired array at dawn—faint, fragmented, probably old. Danse was out of his bunk before the second burst finished.

So was I.

Rhys began checking weapons. Haylen isolated the frequency.

Danse gave orders with machine precision until he reached me.

“You’re staying here.”

“No.”

His head snapped toward me.

“This is a Brotherhood matter.”

“Yesterday ArcJet was a Brotherhood matter.”

“That was different.”

“How?”

His jaw tightened.

“You had been contracted for a specific objective.”

“And today?”

“Today I don’t know what we’re walking into.”

I understood before he finished.

Not policy.

Fear.

He had told me about losing people. Now there was a chance to lose another, and his solution was to remove the variable before it could hurt him.

“You don’t get to tell me something painful and then start deciding my risks for me.”

The station went very quiet.

Rhys became intensely interested in the same rifle part for almost a full minute.

Danse lowered his voice.

“We’ll discuss this outside.”

“Excellent idea.”

We stepped onto the cracked front steps.

Morning fog hung over Cambridge.

Danse turned on me.

“You are not a member of my unit.”

“Correct.”

“I am not obligated to bring you into danger.”

“Also correct.”

“Then what exactly is the problem?”

“The part where you pretend that means you’re entitled to keep me out of it.”

He stared.

I softened my voice.

“Danse. I heard what you said about losing people. I’m not making fun of it. I’m not treating it lightly.”

His anger thinned.

“But I am not one of your dead soldiers waiting to happen.”

His face closed.

“That is not what I said.”

“No. It’s what you’re doing.”

Wind moved through the ruined street.

His eyes went past me toward the barricades where I had first met him.

“I make decisions based on risk.”

“So do I.”

“And if yours is wrong?”

“Then it’s mine.”

He looked back at me.

That landed harder than anything else.

The Brotherhood had given him responsibility for lives. The Commonwealth had taught me ownership of mine. Neither instinct was evil.

They were simply going to collide.

Finally Danse exhaled.

“Stay on my right flank.”

I smiled.

“Six feet?”

“Approximately.”

“Look at us. Compromise.”

“Do not make me regret it.”

“Impossible. You regret everything in advance.”

His mouth twitched.

We went back inside to gear up.

At the door he stopped me with one hand on my shoulder.

“If I order a retreat—”

“I retreat.”

“Immediately.”

“Yes.”

He studied my face as if checking for sarcasm.

There was none.

“Thank you.”

The transmitter was dead, exactly as Danse had predicted. The three ferals inside the relay station were not.

He signaled for the north entrance without speaking. I took the position we'd agreed on, six feet to his right, where I could see the service corridor without blocking his firing line. The first ghoul struck a cabinet and knocked a tray of old ceramic insulators onto the concrete. The crash brought another from a room we hadn't inspected.

“Two contacts,” I called.

“Three. Far door,” Danse answered.

I saw the third shape through the broken glass, moving toward the stairwell rather than us. There was a frightened scavenger halfway down the steps, caught between turning back and running. Danse turned his armor to shield the opening.

“Withdrawal route, east,” he ordered. “Jasper, cover the door. The civilian goes first.”

I didn't argue about the word *civilian*. I covered the corridor and guided the scavenger past the broken electrical cabinet. A shard of metal caught my sleeve, leaving a narrow tear. Danse saw it and went rigid.

“Are you hit?”

“No. Cloth.”

“Confirm.”

I showed him my arm without setting down the rifle. He looked at the clean skin, then nodded once. We finished the retreat without anyone playing hero. The ghouls stayed behind the reinforced door. There was no technology left to recover, and Danse logged the site as unsafe for unarmored entry.

Outside, the scavenger tried to thank him. Danse asked whether they had somewhere safe to go. When they said yes, he gave them the approved route to the settlement and made no promises about a Brotherhood escort he hadn't been authorized to provide.

I waited until they left.

“You wanted to order me behind you.”

“Yes,” he said.

“You didn't.”

“The position was yours.”

“And the order to retreat?”

“Was mine. You followed it.”

I looked at the torn sleeve, then at him. The agreement had survived danger, which was more than our conversation in a quiet office could have proved.



The argument mattered anyway.

It was the first time Danse let me choose danger after he had admitted I mattered enough for the choice to frighten him.
